name: Lurong (velvet antler)

card.summary: The soft, uncalcified antler of deer, used as a traditional Chinese tonic and modern supplement, taken for vitality, joint and bone support, recovery and skin and hair qualities.
card.aka: Cornu cervi pantotrichum, deer antler velvet, lurong
card.note: Deer antler sprays have been linked to contamination and banned-substance controversies in sport.

quick.overview:
Lurong is the Chinese name for velvet antler, the young, hair-covered antler of deer such as sika and red deer, cut before it hardens. In traditional Chinese medicine it is a tonic for yang deficiency, and today it is sold as powders, capsules, extracts and sprays.

For appearance, the claimed chain runs through joint and bone support, recovery and vitality: feeling and training better, which can mean more training and a fuller physique. Human research is limited and mostly concerns arthritis, exercise hormones and bone-related formulas.
quick.how: Traditionally it is boiled into soups as dried slices or powder or made into an alcohol extract. Modern forms include capsules, powder and sprays, often sold by deer farms in New Zealand and elsewhere. In the Korean and Chinese trade, tips, middle and base sections are valued differently.
quick.risks: Limited safety data exists. The FDA has warned sellers about disease-treatment claims, and sports bodies have flagged contamination and IGF-1 concerns in sprays. A rower study found no change in hormone response. Products used for bone or hormone conditions should be discussed with a clinician.

lead: Lurong, or velvet antler (Cornu cervi pantotrichum), is the soft, velvet-covered antler of deer harvested while still growing and before it calcifies [1]. In traditional Chinese medicine it is associated with yang-deficiency conditions and with growth, joint, bone and vitality claims [1]. It is sold as a dietary supplement in several countries.

People take it for general vigor, joint comfort, recovery and, in some marketing, skin, hair and physique benefits. The chain is indirect: if it helps joints and recovery, a person may train more, and with it improve muscle and body composition. Deer antler is also a model for regeneration research because it is the fastest-growing mammalian tissue and rarely forms tumors [2].

Clinical research is limited: a randomized trial in rheumatoid arthritis, a rower study of hormone responses and meta-analyses of Chinese herbal formulas containing velvet antler [3][4][5]. A 2012 review cited on Wikipedia found health claims not supported by sound human trial data [1].

chain: Velvet antler taken as tonic or supplement
Joint comfort, recovery and vitality claimed
More training and a fuller physique, plus skin and hair claims
angle.text: Users take velvet antler as a traditional tonic and sports supplement for joint, bone and recovery support. Marketing links this to better training and a healthier look, a chain that has not been demonstrated in human trials.

paras: Velvet antler is the whole antler at an early, uncalcified stage, covered in soft hairy skin. It is dried, powdered or made into an alcohol-based extract [1]. Antlers are cut near the base after about 55 to 65 days of growth, and in New Zealand deer receive local anesthesia under veterinary supervision [1].

Lurong is used in boiled soups in traditional Chinese medicine, and antlers are sorted into tip, middle and base sections linked to different supposed benefits, including growth in children and joint and bone health in older people [1]. Chinese prescriptions combine it with herbs for bone conditions and gynecological complaints, and formulas such as Fufang Lurong Jiangu capsule have been studied in osteoporosis models [6]. Russia produced an alcohol extract called Pantocrin from the 1930s to the 1980s [1].

A 168-person, six-month randomized, triple-blind trial examined elk velvet antler in rheumatoid arthritis with residual symptoms, measuring joint pain, function and C-reactive protein [3]. An earlier phase II trial of 40 patients assessed safety alongside standard medication [7]. A trial in male and female rowers examined hormonal responses to exercise with elk velvet antler supplementation [4]. A systematic review of Chinese herbal prescriptions containing Ejiao or velvet antler for uterine fibroids pooled nine randomized trials of 844 patients and reported greater fibroid-volume reduction when combined with mifepristone [5].

Reviews describe antlers as the fastest-growing animal tissue, growing about 2 cm a day while rarely becoming cancerous, which has prompted regeneration studies [2]. Peptides derived from velvet antler proteins have been examined for anti-inflammatory properties in laboratory work [8].

Deer antler spray gained attention in sport. A linebacker won a $5.4 million judgment against the maker after a positive test for methyltestosterone, MLB banned the spray in 2011 and WADA warned that products might contain IGF-1. Endocrinologists quoted say sprays contain too little IGF-1 to matter [1]. The FDA has sent warning letters over disease claims, and sale as a supplement is allowed without disease claims [1].

timeline.event: Russia begins producing Pantocrin, an antler extract, in use until the 1980s [1].
WADA lifts its ban but warns of IGF-1 risk; the Alabama attorney general closes S.W.A.T.S. [1].
